content.text: In a tool-use loop, a thinking block isn't leftover output: it's part of the response Claude is still building, and the API expects it back with the tool result, unchanged. Rebuilding or filtering the latest assistant message returns a 400. On Claude 5.1 and later models, which include Claude Opus 5.5, each block is also bound to everything sent before it, so editing earlier history invalidates it. Append turns exactly as received, and let the server trim.
Your incident agent runs on Claude Opus 5.5 with two tools,
. To keep requests small, a helper "cleans" the history before every call: it keeps only the
blocks of each assistant turn, since the thinking blocks come back with an empty

field anyway, and it cuts old log results to 2,000 characters. Every test passes on your API key: the test incidents are simple, and adaptive thinking can skip thinking on simple requests. Then a customer runs the agent on a real outage, and the second request fails with a 400: thinking blocks "in the latest assistant message cannot be modified".
"Thinking blocks are disposable output, so you can drop or edit them in the history to save tokens during tool use." It sounds like ordinary context hygiene:

items.text: field is empty by default, so the block looks like dead weight.
The thinking is about steps Claude already took; the tool calls and the answer seem to be what matters.
Outside tool use, the docs do allow leaving out earlier turns' thinking.
Long histories cost input tokens, and trimming old content is a standard way to keep an agent cheap.

content.text: The half-truth: outside a tool loop you may omit earlier turns' thinking, and the API already filters what each model needs. But inside a tool loop the thinking block belongs to an unfinished response, and on current models every block is tied to the exact history that came before it.
A tool loop is one assistant turn

From the model's side, the assistant turn ends only when Claude finishes its full response, and every tool call and result in between belongs to that turn. The docs explain why the reasoning must come back: "When Claude calls a tool, it pauses construction of its response to await external information. When you return the tool result, Claude continues building that same response, so its earlier reasoning must still be present." Their rule of thumb has three levels: within a tool-use turn, passing

back is required; across turns, passing everything back is recommended; outside tool use, omitting prior turns' thinking is allowed. The same turn also has to run in one thinking mode, so change thinking settings between turns, not inside a loop.
An empty thinking field isn't an empty block
field is an empty string, but "the

field still carries the encrypted full thinking for multi-turn continuity". You also paid for that reasoning already: "You're still charged for the full thinking tokens. Omitting reduces latency, not cost." Opus 5.5 can also write short progress updates between tool calls, and each one arrives as another
block with its own signature. All of them go back with the turn.
The API checks what you send back
Two checks catch an edited history. First, the latest assistant message must match what the API returned: you can't rearrange, edit or partially drop its thinking blocks,
included. A message rebuilt by your code or filtered by block type fails with a 400 whose message contains "
blocks in the latest assistant message cannot be modified".
Second, on Claude 5.1 and later models the API checks each block's prefix: the
, and every message before the block. If any of them changed since the block was produced, that block and every later one fail. Shortening an old

is exactly such an edit. On Claude Opus 5.5, an account created on or after August 31, 2026 gets a 400 that says the block "is bound to a different conversation"; an older account gets no error. Retrying the same body fails the same way every time.
The first version filters each assistant turn and trims old results. The second sends every turn back as it came:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": INCIDENT}]
while True:
    reply = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000,
                                   tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    # "Thinking comes back empty on Opus 5.5: keep only what matters"
    kept = [b for b in reply.content if b.type in ("text", "tool_use")]
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": kept})
    if reply.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    shorten_old_tool_results(messages, limit=2000)  # "save tokens"
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": run_tools(reply)})
print(next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text"))

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": INCIDENT}]
while True:
    reply = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000,
                                   tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    # Echo the turn exactly: thinking, progress updates, text, tool_use
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply.content})
    if reply.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": run_tools(reply)})
print(next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text"))

content.text: On a hard incident, the first version fails on its second request: Claude thought before calling a tool, and the filtered turn no longer matches the one the API sent. Even if it didn't, the trimmed log would invalidate every later thinking block on newer accounts.

content.text: Accounts created before August 31, 2026 get no error when a block fails the prefix check; newer accounts get a 400. The docs warn that people running your tool with their own API keys "can get a 400 error even when you don't". In tests, send the
so your key fails the way theirs will.
